title: Pricing by hours per project for Pet and house sitting
audience: Pet and house sitters who write quotes for visits and stays and need a price that covers cost and earns a margin.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the owner's own figures
Estimate project hours, including set-up, travel and checking time
Build a quote from hours, a rate and a margin, and state its basis and exclusions

instruction.heading: Why hours are the starting unit
instruction.body: A visit to feed and walk a dog takes more time than the time on site: the drive, the key handover, the logbook and the message to the owner. An overnight stay has hours that do not fit a visit rate, because you are on call, you sleep in the home and you may be woken. Start from hours so that each form of stay has a visible cost. Vendor day rates (Dogster, 18 October 2026) do not show how many hours they assume, so they cannot tell you what your own time costs.

instruction.heading: Build the cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Add the year's costs: vehicle running costs, insurance, phone and booking-platform fees, consumables such as litter, bags and treats, any registration fee, administration and training. Divide by productive hours: time spent caring for animals or visiting homes, not the hours you are on call or travelling between jobs. Decide now how you will count the hours of an overnight stay, and record that rule with the figure. Platform fees are a cost. A Rover help-centre page, which is a UK page with no date shown, says sitters keep 85 per cent of earnings from each booking. That figure is Rover's and is not confirmed for Australia, so count the fee before you divide.

instruction.heading: Estimate the hours
instruction.body: Break each booking into visits, travel between visits and to the home, the key handover and close-up, the logbook and the daily report. Use a standard time for each visit length, and record the actual minutes. Add a named allowance for delays, such as a late owner or a dog that needs a vet. Xero's small-business guide suggests 10 to 20 per cent for unexpected work (Xero Australia, 3 September 2026). That is a general figure, not a pet-sitting figure, so size your own from records.

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the productive hours by your cost per productive hour, add a margin that reflects the risk (an unfamiliar home, a dog with medical needs or a long drive), and apply your minimum charge. Show any platform fee as a cost, not as a deduction from your margin. If the owner asks for a lower price, show which visits or which days they are asking you to remove. That keeps the discussion on the work rather than on the person.

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest
instruction.body: A quote states the dates, the visit times, the animals, the owner's duties (feeding, medication, vet authority and access), the exclusions and how long the quote is valid. Do not show your internal cost per hour unless you choose to. Re-quote when the number of animals or visits changes. No Australian holiday or peak-season price source was found, so do not add a peak figure from this lesson.

instruction.heading: Review your estimates
instruction.body: Compare estimated and actual minutes for at least the first ten bookings of each type. If the gap stays above an agreed threshold, change the standard time, the margin or the overnight rule. A pricing method is finished when actual minutes match quoted minutes closely enough for each booking to make money.

procedure: Gather the year's business costs and the productive hours in the same period, and record how you count an overnight stay.
Divide total costs by productive hours to get the cost per productive hour.
Break each booking into visits, travel, handover, logbook and report time, using standard times as ranges.
Add a named allowance for delays and size it from your own records.
Multiply the hours by the cost per hour, add the margin, count any platform fee as a cost, and apply the minimum charge.
Write the quote with dates, visit times, owner duties, exclusions and validity, then record actual minutes after each booking.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only, not market rates. A sitter in Melbourne is offered a five-night stay with two dogs and two visits a day. Each visit takes 30 minutes on site and 15 minutes of travel. Handover and logbook work add 1 hour across the stay. Her cost per productive hour is $35 (illustrative), and her target margin on price is 25 per cent (illustrative). She counts the overnight duties separately.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the price for the visits alone, and what changes if she counts 2 productive hours a night for overnight duties?
workedExamples.reasoning: The ten visits take 5 hours on site, and the travel adds 2.5 hours, which is 7.5 hours, plus the 1 hour of handover and logbook work, so the visit time is 8.5 hours. The cost is 8.5 hours multiplied by $35, which is $297.50. A 25 per cent margin on price gives a price of $396.67. If she counts 2 productive hours for each of the five nights, that adds 10 hours and $350 of cost, so the cost becomes $647.50 and the price becomes $863.33. A platform fee would be a further cost and would need its own line; the fee rate is not confirmed for Australia. Nothing in this example is a sourced price.

equipmentAndPpe: Quote worksheet with visit lengths and standard times
Time log for each booking, with estimated and actual minutes
Logbook template for visits and the daily report
Written permission form for keys and home access (a practice point)

commonErrors.error: Pricing from a daily rate alone
commonErrors.prevention: Count visit, travel and admin hours, and state how overnight time is counted.

commonErrors.error: Counting on-call or travelling time as productive hours
commonErrors.prevention: Use the time spent caring for animals or visiting homes only.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out travel and handover time
commonErrors.prevention: Add these as named lines on every quote.

commonErrors.error: Quoting with no exclusions or owner duties
commonErrors.prevention: List exclusions, owner duties and access assumptions on every quote.

commonErrors.error: Never comparing estimates with actual minutes
commonErrors.prevention: Record actual minutes and review the difference every month.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Pricing guidance only. The Australian Consumer Law applies to pricing statements, and the ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited (15 July 2026). State and territory rules also apply and differ.

Victorian in-home pet sitting rules are UNRESOLVED in this research. Victoria's boarding code and the Domestic Animal Business registration may or may not cover a sitter's own home. Ask the council before you set a price structure for a Victorian service.
No Australian source on key-holding consent or home-access rules was found. Written consent is a good practice step, not a sourced legal requirement.
Pay rates and on-costs for any employee may be set by an award or enterprise agreement. Check which applies before using any wage figure. This lesson does not state those rates.

qualityStandard: Each quote shows dates, visit times, owner duties, exclusions and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the sitter's own records and dated.
Actual minutes are recorded for at least the first ten bookings of each type.
Overnight time is counted by a written rule, applied the same way each time.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet with the source of each figure
Quote with dates, visit times, owner duties and exclusions
Booking time log with estimated and actual minutes
Written permission for keys and home access, dated
summary: Start each quote from visit and travel time, and say how overnight time is counted.
Count only the hours spent caring for animals or visiting homes when you work out cost per productive hour.
Treat platform fees as a cost, and check Victorian rules with the council.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour for a pet sitter?
options: Only the owner's payment for the stay and any late fee charged
The average daily rate of competitors listed on a platform
Only the sitter's pay from the last booking
Vehicle, insurance, phone and booking fees, consumables, registration and admin, divided by productive hours

knowledgeChecks.question: A stay is estimated at 6 hours and takes 9. What is the right response?
options: Record the actual minutes, find the cause, and adjust the estimate and future quotes
Leave the estimate, since the owner has paid and the stay is finished
Reduce the visits for the next owner and skip the logbook
Raise the price for this owner only and no one else is charged more

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a sitting quote need an exclusions list and owner duties?
options: To hide the margin from the owner
To show what the price covers, so changes can be priced and disputes are reduced
To make the stay seem smaller than it is
